In paper 3, SkipGram uses Hierarchical Softmax when the output vocabulary is large and a full softmax would be too expensive; the model replaces the flat normalization over all words with a binary tree, so predicting a target word requires only O(log |V|) decisions along a root-to-leaf path. In the word2vec setting, this is the standard efficiency trick used for training SkipGram on large corpora.

Paper 2 (node2vec) argues that a single notion of neighborhood is not enough for graphs that contain both homophily-based communities and structural-equivalence roles. To address this, it designs a biased random-walk neighborhood sampler that can interpolate between breadth-first-like exploration, which stays near the source and captures community structure, and depth-first-like exploration, which moves outward and captures nodes with similar structural positions. This motivates learning embeddings from neighborhoods that are not fixed a priori, but are adaptively sampled to reflect either local community context or broader structural similarity depending on the walk bias.
confidence_reasoning: These points are standard descriptions of hierarchical softmax in word2vec/SkipGram and of node2vec’s BFS-vs-DFS biased random-walk motivation, so I am highly confident, though exact wording may vary by paper.
